consensus_summary: The consensus identifies Gospel primarily as the good news (euangelion) of salvation through Jesus Christ’s death for sins, burial, resurrection, and the related inauguration of God’s kingdom, grounded especially in 1 Cor 15:1-4, Rom 1:16-17, and Mark 1:14-15 (with Isa 52:7 as OT background). Kingdom emphasis, the four written Gospels as literary genre, and secondary social/liberation or imperial readings are recognized alternatives or emphases rather than replacements of the core.
book_summary: The book defines Gospel as “the gospel of the kingdom — the renewed covenant, the law going forth from Zion,” while explicitly noting the common teaching as the good news that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again.
consensus_core_identification: good news of salvation/kingdom accomplished through Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection
book_core_identification: gospel of the kingdom identified as the renewed covenant and the law going forth from Zion
boundary_disagreement: The book retains the “gospel of the kingdom” category present in consensus alternatives but reclassifies its defining content away from the cross-resurrection summary (1 Cor 15) toward the new-covenant promise and the law/word issuing from Zion, thereby excluding or demoting the atonement-centered cases that the consensus treats as primary.
material_contradiction: None; the book’s identification remains within the recognized kingdom/Isaianic strand and does not assert that the consensus referent is false, only that a different specification is correct.
rationale: Minimum cores share the “gospel of the kingdom / good news of God’s reign” category attested across the consensus responses (especially the kingdom and Isaianic-restoration alternatives). The book therefore does not replace the general referent. It does, however, materially narrow and re-precision that referent by equating it specifically to the renewed covenant (Jer 31) plus the law going forth from Zion (Isa 2:3), a boundary shift that reclassifies the 1 Cor 15 formulation from primary definition to merely “commonly taught.” This is refinement of extension and precision, not core contradiction or novelty.
strongest_objection: The most explicit NT definitional texts (1 Cor 15:1-4; Rom 1:16) center the gospel on Christ’s death and resurrection for sins; equating it instead with “the law going forth from Zion” appears to reverse the Pauline gospel/law distinction and lacks a direct scriptural equation.
